about.title: Salinas Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Something you bought is supposed to work. When a space heater, a car seat, a power tool, or a prescription bottle instead leaves you hurt, California law doesn't ask you to prove the company was careless. In most product cases it asks a simpler question: was the product defective, and did that defect cause your injury? That is strict liability, and it applies to three kinds of flaws: how the item was designed, how a particular unit was made, and whether the warnings or instructions were adequate. For a Salinas household, that matters in practical ways. Keep the product. Don't return it, don't let the store swap it out, and don't throw away the box, receipt, or manual. Photograph the failure and write down where and when you bought it. Everyone in the chain, from the manufacturer to the distributor to the Monterey County retailer who sold it, may share responsibility. LawProactive is not a law firm. We simply connect you, at no cost, with an independent attorney who handles product claims on contingency, so there's no fee unless there's a recovery.

items.title: Strict Liability Changes the Question
items.desc: In California you usually don't have to show the maker was negligent, only that the product was defective and caused your harm. An attorney in our network can explain which defect theory fits your situation.

items.title: Three Kinds of Defects, One Claim
items.desc: Design flaws, manufacturing errors, and inadequate warnings are each grounds for a claim. The attorney you're connected with can help pin down which one applies to the item that hurt you.

items.title: Every Link in the Chain Counts
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and the Salinas retailer that sold the product may all be held responsible under California law. Identifying each party early can matter, and it costs nothing to be connected with an attorney who will look.

items.question: I bought the product at a store in Salinas but it was made overseas. Who is responsible?
items.answer: California law lets an injured person look to everyone who placed the product into the stream of commerce, not just the original maker. That can include the importer, the distributor, and the local retailer where you purchased it. An independent attorney can sort out which parties are reachable in your case.

items.question: Could a defective vehicle part have played a role in my Salinas crash?
items.answer: It's possible. Salinas recorded 410 injury collisions in 2025, and some crashes involve a failed component such as a tire, brake, or airbag rather than driver error alone. If you suspect equipment failure, keep the vehicle from being repaired or scrapped until an attorney can arrange an inspection.

items.question: What should I do with the product that hurt me?
items.answer: Hold on to it, along with any packaging, instructions, and proof of purchase. Do not return it to the store or accept a replacement, because the item itself is often the strongest piece of evidence. Store it safely and unaltered until you've spoken with an attorney.
